title: Writing an essay
goal: Build a formal Indonesian essay the way an editor expects it: paragraphs with a clear *kalimat utama*, sentences linked by the right cohesion markers, and a *simpulan* that ends rather than repeats.
bekal: write a paragraph with a *kalimat utama* and *kalimat penjelas*, deductive or inductive
link sentences and paragraphs with *selain itu, sebaliknya, oleh karena itu, dengan kata lain*
turn spoken sentence openers (*Dan, Tapi, Makanya, Soalnya*) into written ones

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Paragraf pertama
dialogs.intro: Late November 2029, a wet evening in Jakarta. Mbak Dewi has invited Sarah to write an opinion piece for her newspaper. Dr. Lestari has stayed late at the Program Jembatan office to look at the first draft.

lines.text: Bu, Mbak Dewi minta esai delapan ratus kata untuk rubrik opini. Temanya pengalaman belajar bahasa Indonesia.

lines.speaker: Lestari:
lines.text: Simpan untuk paragraf lain. Lalu, antarparagraf perlu penghubung: “selain itu”, “sebaliknya”, “oleh karena itu”.
lines.id: Save it for another paragraph. And between paragraphs you need linking words: “in addition”, “conversely”, “therefore”.

notes: **Rubrik opini** — the opinion column of a newspaper. *Rubrik* is any regular section (*rubrik olahraga*, *rubrik budaya*). Indonesian dailies publish outside contributors' essays constantly, and *menulis di kolom opini Kompas* is a real mark of standing.

**Boleh saya bacakan?** — "may I read (it) for you?" The *-kan* of *bacakan* is the benefactive you met in A2 Unit 5: *membacakan* is to read aloud for someone. The object-focus order, *boleh saya bacakan*, is the polite way to offer.

**Kalimat utama and kalimat penjelas** — topic sentence and supporting sentences. Indonesian schools drill this from primary level, and every editor thinks in these terms. *Gagasan pokok* (main idea) is what the *kalimat utama* states.

**Deduktif, induktif** — a deductive paragraph opens with the *kalimat utama*; an inductive one builds up to it at the end; a *campuran* (mixed) one states it at the start and restates it at the end. Opinion pieces in the Indonesian press are overwhelmingly deductive.
**Sayang sekali, padahal…** — *padahal* ("whereas, and yet") adds the fact that makes the loss painful. *Sayang* here is "a pity", not "darling"; context always tells you which.

**Simpulan or kesimpulan?** Both mean "conclusion" and both are in KBBI. Language teachers and style guides prefer *simpulan* for the conclusion of a text, keeping *kesimpulan* for the act or result of concluding. Most people use *kesimpulan* for everything; in a test, write *simpulan*.

grammars.title: Anatomy of a paragraph
body: An Indonesian textbook paragraph has named parts, and an editor will use these names when commenting on your draft.
after: The test of a *kalimat penjelas* is simple: does it support the *kalimat utama*? If not, it belongs elsewhere or nowhere, like Sarah's eleventh floor.
Aim for four to six sentences a paragraph in an opinion piece. A one-sentence paragraph is a journalistic effect; use it once, at most.

grammars.title: Cohesion markers
body: These are the *penghubung* (linking words) that carry a reader from one sentence or paragraph to the next. Each opens a sentence and is followed by a comma.

head: Function
Markers
English
rows: *Selain itu, Di samping itu, Lebih lanjut*
In other words, In short, In the end

after: ⚠️ *Sehingga* and *karena* join clauses inside one sentence; they cannot open a sentence on their own. *Sehingga acaranya ditunda.* is a fragment. Write *Oleh karena itu, acaranya ditunda.* instead.
⚠️ *Daripada* is only for comparison (*lebih sering mengangguk daripada memahami*), never as a linking word meaning "of" or "than that".

dialogs.title: Second dialogue — Catatan dari redaksi
dialogs.intro: Four days later. Mbak Dewi calls Sarah about the draft she sent in.

lines.text: Mbak Sarah, esainya sudah saya baca. Secara keseluruhan bagus, dan kami akan memuatnya Sabtu depan.

notes: **Memuat** — literally "to load, contain", and the standard verb for a newspaper publishing something: *Kompas memuat esainya*, *Esainya dimuat hari Sabtu*. *Menerbitkan* is used for books and whole publications.

**Secara keseluruhan** — "on the whole". *Secara* + noun or adjective makes an adverb phrase: *secara umum* (in general), *secara resmi* (officially), *secara pribadi* (personally). Editors love to open with praise *secara keseluruhan* before the notes.

**Pertama, kedua, yang ketiga** — Dewi numbers her points, which is how Indonesians give structured feedback. Sarah's *Yang ketiga?* ("and the third one?") uses *yang* to stand for the missing noun, *catatan*.
**Ragam tulis** — written register, as opposed to *ragam lisan* (spoken register). *Ragam* means "variety"; it is the same root as *beragam* and *keberagaman* from Unit 17.

**Memancing rasa ingin tahu** — "to arouse curiosity", literally "to fish for the feeling of wanting to know". *Memancing* (to fish) is used for provoking anything: *memancing emosi* (to provoke anger), *memancing diskusi*.

**Mengira** vs **berpikir.** *Mengira* is "to suppose, assume", usually wrongly: *Saya kira dia sudah pulang* (I thought he'd gone home, but he hadn't). *Pembaca mengira* is exactly the misunderstanding Sarah fears.

grammars.title: From spoken openers to written ones
body: Speech happily starts sentences with *dan*, *tapi* or *makanya*. Written Indonesian replaces each with a full cohesion marker followed by a comma.
after: *Tetapi* and *dan* are perfectly good inside a sentence: *Kalimatnya jernih, tetapi paragrafnya belum punya kalimat utama.* The rule is only about the first word after a full stop.
*Jadi* is acceptable in semi-formal writing and in speeches; in an essay or report, *oleh karena itu* or *dengan demikian* reads more deliberately.

sections.title: The shape of an opinion essay

blocks.text: An 800-word *esai opini* has three parts. The proportions below are what Indonesian editors expect, give or take a paragraph.

head: Part
Share
What it does
Sample opening
rows: hooks the reader, states the issue
*Empat tahun lalu, saya hanya tahu dua kata.*
*Pertama, bahasa Indonesia memaksa saya memperhatikan nada.*
*Selain itu, bahasa ini mengajari saya menunggu.*
*Meskipun demikian, tidak semua diam itu setuju.*
*Pada akhirnya, belajar bahasa adalah belajar rendah hati.*

blocks.text: *Pendahuluan, isi, penutup* are the words teachers and editors use; you will also see *bagian awal, bagian inti, bagian akhir*. A good title (*judul*) is short, specific and has a verb or a surprise in it.
Here is the paragraph after Lestari's advice: a mixed (*campuran*) paragraph that states the idea, supports it three times and restates it.

head: Sentence
Role
rows: *Bahasa Indonesia mengajari saya satu hal yang tidak saya duga: mendengarkan.*
*Empat tahun lalu, di sebuah kantor di Jakarta, saya lebih sering mengangguk daripada memahami.*
*Karena belum lancar, saya terpaksa memperhatikan nada, jeda, dan wajah lawan bicara.*
*Dari situ saya belajar bahwa “iya” tidak selalu berarti setuju.*
*Kemudian saya sadar bahwa dalam bahasa Inggris pun saya jarang mendengarkan sesabar itu.*
*Dengan kata lain, bahasa baru membuat saya menjadi pendengar yang lebih baik.*

blocks.text: In English: “Indonesian taught me one thing I did not expect: listening. Four years ago, in an office in Jakarta, I nodded more often than I understood. Because I was not yet fluent, I had to pay attention to tone, pauses and the other person's face. From that I learnt that *iya* does not always mean yes. Then I realised that even in English I seldom listened so patiently. In other words, a new language made me a better listener.”
Cover the Indonesian column, read the English, and rebuild each sentence from memory.

head: English
Indonesian
rows: Early February? Oh, that's right on Lebaran. In 2030 Idul Fitri falls in early February.
*Awal Februari? Wah, Mbak, itu pas Lebaran. Tahun 2030 Idul Fitri jatuhnya awal Februari.*
OK, we'll move the arrival to mid-February, after the collective leave days.
*Oke, kedatangan kita geser ke pertengahan Februari, setelah cuti bersama.*
Then we'll move Bali to April. When's Waisak?

Miss Sarah, may I ask something a bit personal?

Oh, sorry, Miss. Here it's normal, you know. It's even on our ID cards.
*Oh, maaf, Miss. Di sini kan biasa. Di KTP juga ada.*
